meta.title: TurtleLab Lessons
meta.caveat: Aligned by reading the five steps' own text; nothing a learner makes has been checked against these yet. Locators are the steps' URL slugs (/turtle-lessons/<slug>/). The sequence is short and starts from samples, so loops, if and else, and random are the real fits, and most other entries are partial or related. Variables and procedures show up only as optional or read-only material (Step 5's Done early, the letter blocks in Step 1's samples), so they are marked related. Only the four computer science and CTE frameworks were examined. CSTA 2017 is a legacy framework and was left out, as in the Pico carriers. Common Core math has a coordinate plane code (6.NS.6) that Step 1 fits, but it is not included because the lesson widget does not show math standards.

alignment_log.scope: First pass: all five steps against apcsp, castandards, csta2026 and ca-ict-anchor
alignment_log.note: Read each step's student text and matched it against this repo's catalog paraphrases. Kept strong to loops, if and else, random, and run to run variation; most others are partial. Two CTE codes only (C4.9 and 5.9), on purpose, because the CTE anchors are broad and little of this sequence needs them. Candidates left out as too thin: 5.12 (Boolean logic and decisions, Step 4 only), 5.7 (working through a problem repeatedly), C5.5 (evaluating a result against its requirements), apcsp 3.16 (simulations, since no step calls the random walk one).

1.2.note: Steps 2, 3 and 4 each ask what a program will do before it runs, and why: the ring of 36 dashes, the 50 rays, which way the turtle turns for each answer. That is explaining what a code segment does when it runs. Input and output as named ideas are not taught.

locator_notes.step-2-say-it-once: Work out what a loop of 36 turns of 10 adds up to before changing it.
locator_notes.step-3-let-chance-draw: Guess whether a second run will match the first, then explain why 50 rays turning 7.2 each close the circle.
locator_notes.step-4-choose-a-path: Say which way the turtle turns for each answer to the question, and whether both or neither can run.

1.3.note: Step 5 follows a small development process: sketch the picture, finish three plan sentences, build in three pieces and run after each, then check the result against a list. A sticky note in the program says what it does. Step 1 starts the same habit with a paper plan and one letter at a time. There is no gathering of requirements from other people, and no crediting of other people's code.

locator_notes.step-1-your-initials: Plan the initials on paper first, then build and test one letter at a time. The sticky note holds only a name.
locator_notes.step-5-random-art: Sketch, three plan sentences, build in small pieces, check against a list, and a sticky note that says what the loop, the random and the if and else do.

1.4.note: Each of these steps gives a way to find and fix a mistake: predict and compare with what the turtle does (Step 1), trace by hand with chosen inputs and a known answer (Step 4), and the troubleshooting list in Step 5 (read the message, change one number at a time, undo). Kinds of errors such as syntax and logic errors are not named.

locator_notes.step-1-your-initials: Predict where the L ends and which way it faces, run it, and compare.
locator_notes.step-4-choose-a-path: Trace six chosen coin flips by hand and check the headings against the answers. A red outline on the if block marks the problem.
locator_notes.step-5-random-art: A short list for when something is not working: read the message, change one number at a time, stop, undo.

3.1.note: Only in Done early at the end of Step 5, where the Square spiral sample keeps a number in a box that grows each time through the loop. It is optional, so the steps do not count on it.

locator_notes.step-5-random-art: Optional: read how box1 grows in the Square spiral sample, then use a box in your own picture.

3.3.note: Step 1 is about sequencing: the turtle does the steps in the order given and nothing else, so a plan is written as a list of moves before it becomes blocks. Steps 2 and 3 use arithmetic on the page (360 divided by the number of sides, 36 times 10, 50 times 7.2) to decide what to type, but no step asks for expressions built from operators inside the program.

locator_notes.step-1-your-initials: Steps run in order, one after another. Write the moves as a list, then build them.
locator_notes.step-2-say-it-once: Turn equals 360 divided by the number of sides, and 36 loops of 10 degrees make a full circle.
locator_notes.step-3-let-chance-draw: 50 rays turning 7.2 degrees each, and the turn for 100 rays, worked out by hand.

3.4.note: Only the comparison part of this topic (this catalog files relational operators here, next to strings). The if and else question is a comparison that gives yes or no, and Done early uses a less than comparison. Strings are not covered.

locator_notes.step-4-choose-a-path: Only the comparison part of this topic: the question "random 1 2 = 1" is a comparison with a yes or no answer. Strings are not covered.

3.6.note: Step 4 teaches the if and else block: a yes or no question, exactly one of two mouths runs, never both and never neither. It is traced by hand and then used to set a color in each mouth. Step 5 requires one in the capstone. A plain if with no else, and nested conditions, are not taught.

locator_notes.step-4-choose-a-path: Exactly one of the two mouths runs. Trace it on paper, then set a different color in each mouth.
locator_notes.step-5-random-art: The capstone needs an if and else that changes something you can see.

3.8.note: Step 2 is built around the repeat block: the blocks inside run again and again and the number says how many times (a square, then shapes with 3 to 12 sides, then a ring of 36 dashes). Steps 3, 4 and 5 use repeat in the samples and in what you build: 50 rays, 60 pieces of confetti, 120 steps of a walk. Only counted loops are taught; a loop that runs until a condition is met is not.

locator_notes.step-2-say-it-once: The repeat block, how its number and its turn fit together, and a ring of dashes.
locator_notes.step-3-let-chance-draw: A loop of 50 rays, and a loop that scatters 60 dots.
locator_notes.step-4-choose-a-path: A loop of 120 steps with the if and else inside it.
locator_notes.step-5-random-art: The capstone is drawn by a repeat.

3.9.note: You build new programs from pieces you already know. Step 3 changes a sample and then builds confetti from a loop, random places and random colors. Step 5 combines a loop, random and an if and else in a picture of your own. Comparing two algorithms for the same job is not asked.

locator_notes.step-3-let-chance-draw: Adapt a sample, then build confetti by combining a loop, set xy and random.
locator_notes.step-5-random-art: Combine a loop, random and an if and else into one piece of art.

3.13.note: The samples in Step 1 draw each letter with a block of its own, so each letter is easy to find and read and the same block can be used anywhere. Learners read and use them, but the step says they do not need to make their own yet, so writing procedures is not covered.

locator_notes.step-1-your-initials: The sample letters are blocks of their own that start where the turtle is. Reading them is enough for now.

3.15.note: Step 3 is about the random block: both ends of its range can come up, a color needs numbers from 0 to 255, and running again can give a different picture. Step 4 uses a 1 or 2 coin flip to choose a branch, and Step 5 requires random in the capstone.

locator_notes.step-3-let-chance-draw: The smallest and largest numbers random 0 255 can give, and random in a color, a length and a position.
locator_notes.step-4-choose-a-path: A coin flip, random 1 2, chooses which road the turtle takes.
locator_notes.step-5-random-art: The capstone needs something random that you can see by running it twice.

6-8.AP.10.note: Before building, Step 1 has you write each letter's start, direction and moves as a list, and Step 5 has you sketch and finish three plan sentences, plus an outline of the program with gaps to fill. These are plans in plain words, not flowcharts or pseudocode.

locator_notes.step-1-your-initials: Write down where the turtle starts, which way it faces, and the moves, before building.
locator_notes.step-5-random-art: A sketch, three plan sentences, and an outline of the program with gaps to fill.

6-8.AP.12.note: A conditional goes inside a loop with random in it, built up in small steps: first a loop that draws one thing, then random, then the if and else. Compound conditions such as and, or are not used, and nested loops are not taught.

locator_notes.step-4-choose-a-path: The stack puts an if and else inside a repeat.
locator_notes.step-5-random-art: Build the capstone in three pieces: a loop, then random, then the if and else.

6-8.AP.13.note: Step 1 breaks the initials into one letter at a time, each planned and tested before the next, and the samples give each letter its own block. Step 5 builds the capstone in three pieces. Learners do not define procedures of their own.

locator_notes.step-1-your-initials: One letter at a time, planned and tested before the next.
locator_notes.step-5-random-art: A loop first, then random, then the if and else, running after each.

6-8.AP.17.note: Step 4 gives a chosen list of six coin flips and asks for the heading after each, which is a deliberate test input with a known answer. Step 5 asks you to run the program twice to see random at work. There is no wider test plan.

locator_notes.step-4-choose-a-path: Six chosen flips, and a heading to work out after each one.
locator_notes.step-5-random-art: Run it twice and see whether the random part changes the picture.

6-8.AP.19.note: A sticky note in the program says what it does in the maker's own words: one sentence on what the if and else decides (Step 4), and what the loop, the random and the if and else each do (Step 5). It is short, and it travels with the PDF.

locator_notes.step-4-choose-a-path: A sticky note with a name and one sentence on what the if and else decides.
locator_notes.step-5-random-art: A sticky note that says what the loop, the random and the if and else each do.

MS-PRO-RD-17.note: Step 4 traces a loop's coin flips by hand and records the turtle's heading after each one (90, 180, 90, 180, 90, 0). Step 1 asks where the L ends and which way it faces, and Step 2 asks what 36 turns of 10 add up to. Each follows code step by step and says what it leaves behind. Procedures that take inputs are not traced.

locator_notes.step-1-your-initials: Where does the turtle end, and which way does it face, after the L?
locator_notes.step-2-say-it-once: Follow a loop of 36 turns of 10 and say what it adds up to.
locator_notes.step-4-choose-a-path: Pretend six coin flips and write the heading after each.

HS-PRO-RD-17.note: Learners read a sample they did not write and explain its parts: what the random color slots do (Step 3), what each mouth of the if and else does (Step 4), and, in the capstone's sticky note, what their own loop, random and if and else do. The samples are short, so this is the lighter end of the standard.

locator_notes.step-3-let-chance-draw: Explain what random 0 255 in each color slot does.
locator_notes.step-4-choose-a-path: Explain what each mouth of the if and else does.
locator_notes.step-5-random-art: The sticky note says what the loop, the random and the if and else each do.

MS-ALG-PS-03.note: Predict, run, compare is the habit in these steps: where the L ends (Step 1), the turn that closes a shape (Step 2), the headings after six flips (Step 4, with answers to check against). Checking is against numbers the learner works out, not a formal set of test cases.

locator_notes.step-1-your-initials: Write a prediction, run it, and compare.
locator_notes.step-2-say-it-once: Predict the turn that closes each shape, then run it to see whether it does.
locator_notes.step-4-choose-a-path: Check the six headings against the answers.

MS-PRO-PD-12.note: The sample letters in Step 1 are blocks of their own, which is the idea of naming steps so code is easier to read and reuse. Learners read and use them but do not make their own in these steps.

locator_notes.step-1-your-initials: Each sample letter is a named block that draws from wherever the turtle is.

MS-PRO-VD-16.note: Only the optional Done early in Step 5: a box holds a number that grows each time through the loop. The main path does not use variables.

locator_notes.step-5-random-art: Optional: a box that grows each time through the loop.

MS-PRO-TR-19.note: Step 1 and Step 5 each end with a Check yourself list to test the finished program against what it was meant to do, and the sticky note records what it does. No feedback from other people is built in.

locator_notes.step-1-your-initials: A Check yourself list: readable letters, no stray lines, a prediction checked, every letter built by hand.
locator_notes.step-5-random-art: A Check yourself list for the loop, the random, the if and else, two colors and a note.

HS-PRO-TR-19.note: The capstone's Check yourself list tests the finished picture against its plan (a loop, random, an if and else, two colors, a note). A sketch and three plan sentences come first. It is a self check, with no usability or accessibility review.

locator_notes.step-5-random-art: Check the finished picture against the plan before saving the PDF.

HS-ALG-PS-04.note: Step 3 asks whether a second run will match the first, then has you run it and find the random block that causes the change; the confetti is run twice and compared. Step 4 asks the same about the coin flip walk, and the capstone says to run twice and look for a change. The same steps with the same numbers always draw the same picture, and random is what makes them vary.

locator_notes.step-3-let-chance-draw: Will the second picture match the first? Run it three times and find out why.
locator_notes.step-4-choose-a-path: Run the walk three times: are the drawings the same, and why?
locator_notes.step-5-random-art: Run the capstone twice. Does it change?

HS-ALG-PS-02.note: Step 2 opens with a square written out in eight blocks, then shows that one forward and one right said once inside repeat 4 does the same job. It is a shown rewrite, and Step 1's eight block frame is pointed at but not assigned as one. Functions are not part of it.

locator_notes.step-2-say-it-once: Eight blocks written out become one forward and one right inside a repeat.

C4.9.note: Loops are Step 2 and branches are Step 4, and the capstone uses both. Variables appear only as an optional extension in Step 5. Procedures are read in the Step 1 samples but not written, and error recovery and recursion are not covered.

locator_notes.step-5-random-art: A loop and an if and else together in one program.

5.9.note: Step 1 breaks the initials into one letter at a time, and Step 5 breaks the capstone into a loop first, then random, then the if and else, running after each piece.

locator_notes.step-1-your-initials: One letter at a time, planned and tested before the next.
locator_notes.step-5-random-art: Three small pieces, run after each.
